params.question: In a displaced mid-shaft clavicle fracture, which muscle is primarily responsible for pulling the medial fragment upward and posteriorly?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The deltoid acts on the distal fragment along with the weight of the arm, pulling it downward. It does not elevate the medial fragment.
Pectoralis major, together with arm weight, displaces the distal fragment downward and medially. It does not pull the medial fragment upward.
Correct! The trapezius pulls the medial fragment upward and posteriorly, while arm weight and pectoralis major drag the distal fragment down, producing the classic step deformity and shortening.
Biceps brachii acts on the elbow and forearm (flexion and supination) and has no direct attachment to the clavicle. It plays no role in clavicle fracture displacement.

overallFeedback.feedback: The trapezius pulls the medial fragment upward and posteriorly. The distal fragment is displaced downward by the combined effect of arm weight, pectoralis major, and deltoid — producing the shortening and step deformity seen clinically.

Correct! The trapezius elevates the medial fragment while arm weight, pectoralis major, and deltoid depress the distal fragment — this opposing pull creates the visible step deformity and shortening characteristic of displaced mid-shaft clavicle fractures.

params.question: In Neer's subclassification of lateral third clavicle fractures, which type carries the highest non-union risk, approaching 30–40%?

answers.text: Type I — minimal displacement with intact coracoclavicular ligaments

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type I fractures are stable because the coracoclavicular ligaments remain intact, keeping the fragments anchored. Non-union risk is low in this subtype.

answers.text: Type II — displaced fracture with torn coracoclavicular ligaments

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Disruption of the conoid and trapezoid ligaments removes the stabilising anchor to the coracoid process, leaving the fracture unstable and displaced — this drives the 30–40% non-union rate.

answers.text: Type III — fracture extending into the acromioclavicular joint

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type III fractures involve the articular surface of the AC joint but do not carry the highest non-union risk in Neer's classification. Type II, with its ligament disruption, is the high-risk subtype.
This refers to the Allman classification (medial third), not Neer's lateral-third subclassification. Medial fractures are rare and generally stabilised by the costoclavicular ligament.

overallFeedback.feedback: Neer Type II fractures of the lateral third have torn coracoclavicular ligaments (conoid and trapezoid), making the fracture unstable and displaced. This instability drives a 30–40% non-union rate and typically warrants surgical fixation.

Correct! Neer Type II lateral clavicle fractures lose the stabilising effect of the coracoclavicular ligaments, resulting in instability and a non-union rate of 30–40%. This is why operative fixation is usually recommended for this subtype.

params.question: A 28-year-old patient has a minimally displaced mid-shaft clavicle fracture with 1.5 cm of shortening and bone ends still in contact. There is no skin compromise. Which management approach is most appropriate?

answers.text: Broad-arm sling with pendulum exercises starting at two weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! With less than 2 cm shortening, maintained bone contact, and no skin compromise, this fracture has favourable features for non-operative management. Pendulum exercises begin at two weeks, with full physiotherapy after union around six weeks.

The figure-of-eight bandage is no longer recommended. Evidence shows it does not reduce displacement and causes pressure sores in the axilla. A broad-arm sling is the current standard for non-operative management.

Operative fixation is reserved for high-risk features: shortening ≥2 cm, complete displacement, skin tenting, open fractures, bilateral fractures, floating shoulder, or polytrauma. This fracture does not meet those criteria.
Intramedullary nailing is a surgical option reserved for fractures meeting operative indications. This fracture has favourable characteristics and does not warrant surgical intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: With shortening under 2 cm, bone ends still in contact, and no skin compromise, this fracture meets criteria for non-operative management. The standard is a broad-arm sling (not a figure-of-eight bandage), with pendulum exercises from two weeks and full physiotherapy after union.

Correct! This fracture has favourable prognostic features — shortening under 2 cm, bone contact maintained, no skin compromise — so conservative management with a broad-arm sling is appropriate. Remember: figure-of-eight bandages are no longer used.

interactions.label: A 40-year-old smoker sustains a comminuted mid-shaft clavicle fracture with 2.5

params.question: A 40-year-old smoker sustains a comminuted mid-shaft clavicle fracture with 2.5 cm of shortening, managed non-operatively. At five months she reports persistent fracture-site pain and reduced shoulder abduction strength. What is the most likely complication and its definitive management?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Malunion implies the bone has united in a poor position. Here, persistent pain with a mobile fragment at five months suggests the bone has not united at all — this is non-union, not malunion.

Brachial plexus neuropraxia is an acute complication of high-energy injuries, typically presenting immediately. The picture here — persistent pain, reduced strength, and failure to heal at five months in a high-risk fracture — is characteristic of non-union.

answers.text: Subclavian vessel compression by callus — urgent vascular referral

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Callus compression of subclavian vessels is a recognised late complication, but it typically presents with vascular symptoms. The combination of pain, reduced strength, and failure to unite at five months with multiple risk factors points to non-union.

answers.text: Non-union — open reduction, plate fixation, and bone grafting

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct! Smoking, comminution, and shortening >2 cm all predispose to non-union, defined as failure to unite by 4–6 months. Definitive treatment is open reduction, plate fixation, and bone grafting to restore stability and stimulate healing.

overallFeedback.feedback: This patient has multiple non-union risk factors: smoking, comminution, and shortening exceeding 2 cm. Non-union is defined as failure of the bone to unite by 4–6 months. The definitive treatment is open reduction, plate fixation, and bone grafting.

Correct! Multiple risk factors — smoking, comminution, and significant shortening — predispose to non-union. At five months with persistent pain and reduced function, the diagnosis is non-union. Definitive treatment is open reduction, plate fixation, and bone grafting.

interactions.label: A 62-year-old woman with primary knee osteoarthritis reports moderate chronic jo

params.question: A 62-year-old woman with primary knee osteoarthritis reports moderate chronic joint pain that limits her daily activities. She has no history of peptic ulcer disease or renal impairment. Which is the most appropriate first-line analgesic?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: NSAIDs such as diclofenac are the step-up option when paracetamol alone is insufficient for degenerative joint pain. They are not first-line due to gastrointestinal and cardiovascular risks with long-term use.
Even weak opioids like tramadol carry significant dependence risk in chronic conditions such as osteoarthritis. Opioids are rarely appropriate as first-line agents for degenerative pain.

Correct! Paracetamol is the recommended first-line analgesic for degenerative joint pain. It provides effective relief for mild-to-moderate pain with a favourable safety profile compared to NSAIDs and opioids.

Methotrexate is a disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) used in inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid arthritis. It has no role in managing primary osteoarthritis, which is degenerative, not inflammatory.

overallFeedback.feedback: Osteoarthritis is a degenerative condition driven by cartilage loss and secondary synovitis. Paracetamol is the first-line analgesic. NSAIDs are the step-up option when paracetamol is insufficient. DMARDs are for inflammatory arthritis, and opioids carry dependence risk in chronic disease.

Correct! For degenerative joint pain (osteoarthritis), paracetamol is the established first-line agent. NSAIDs are stepped up to when paracetamol is insufficient, and opioids carry dependence risk in chronic disease.
